name: Action
subtitle: Perception → Action → Immediate Feedback
concept: The Action‑Reaction pattern focuses on the real‑time feedback between player input and the game world. Its core is that players control one or more entities through continuous, high‑frequency actions (clicks, swipes, key presses) to dodge obstacles, hit targets, or perform rhythmic moves in a dynamic environment. The underlying structure typically includes input sampling, entity state updates, physics or pseudo‑physics calculations, collision detection, and scoring or survival resolution. Designers must balance input latency against collision tolerance: too low latency feels "stiff," while too high latency erodes immediacy. Likewise, the balance between obstacle density and the player’s skill curve is crucial; excessive density can sap a sense of progression, while sparse density reduces challenge. Speed increases and flow are a double‑edged sword—accelerating too quickly can turn flow into anxiety. Notably, a moderate input lag can actually enhance anticipation by giving players a clearer time window to adjust actions, thereby sharpening their sense of impending events.
role: This pattern is used to create tension and flow. It directly translates the player’s reaction speed, anticipation, and precision into gameplay performance, making it one of the most intuitive and accessible play styles. In hyper‑casual and arcade titles, the action‑reaction pattern essentially constitutes the entire experience.
significance: Mastering the action‑reaction pattern means understanding key design dimensions such as input lag, collision tolerance, and difficulty curves. It is the best entry point for learning real‑time systems, physics simulation, animation, and feedback synchronization, and it underpins many complex mechanics like platforming, bullet‑hell shooting, and rhythm games.
problemsSolved: Provide the shortest feedback loop so players immediately understand what they did
Create sustained tension through variations in speed, density, and rhythm
Lower the learning curve with simple single‑finger/single‑key controls
learningGoals: Understand the timing relationships between input sampling, frame updates, and rendering
Master collision boxes, hit detection, and tolerance design
minimalRules: The player controls a movable entity
Obstacles or targets continuously spawn in the scene
Collisions/hits trigger immediate feedback (score, failure, visual effect)
Game speed or obstacle density increases over time
systemLoopHint: Read input → Update player/object state → Detect collisions → Trigger feedback → Resolve score/survival status → Advance to next frame

combos.effect: Adds resource targets beyond dodging/attacking, shifting player priorities
Transforms performance scores into permanent upgrades, extending lifespan
Synchronizes action windows with musical beats, creating a rhythm game experience

advancedWarnings: Excessive input lag or overly strict collision detection can quickly turn players away
Purely random obstacles may create unsolvable situations; introduce controllable generation algorithms
Rapid speed increases can turn flow into anxiety; monitor difficulty pacing
advancedAlgoRefs: Fixed‑timestep physics updates independent of frame rate
AABB / circle collision detection and spatial partitioning optimization
Procedural obstacle generation and difficulty curve control

intro.what: You keep tapping the screen or keyboard to dodge or hit whatever keeps coming at you — Flappy Bird, Fruit Ninja, and Geometry Dash all run on this rhythm.
intro.feel: Eyes on the screen, fingers on instinct; every input lands an instant result — dodge and you keep going, miss and you restart. Not a second to breathe.
intro.why: This is the underlying structure of every action game — tune the "input → feedback" loop well, and the feel of any action play has its foundation.
